statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, detected xylazine reliably when there was at least the strip's listed amount and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not, so these strips would not show them (Sisco et al., 2024a). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In a laboratory, xylazine test strips showed xylazine in 37 of 38 residue samples that had at least the amount the strip is made to find, and in none of 34 without it. With smaller amounts they often missed it. They did not react to medetomidine, a similar animal sedative. One batch of strips was tested, on scrapings from used equipment rather than on powders.
population: 100 drug residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment in two US states, and pure xylazine and 76 other compounds in water
exposure: One production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips, two strips per sample, read in a laboratory; a later version with a different antibody in a second study
comparator: GC-MS/MS quantitation of xylazine in each residue sample; known content of prepared solutions
outcome: Sensitivity and specificity on residue samples, the lowest concentration giving consistent positives, and reactions to other compounds
magnitude: Sisco et al. (2024a), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). Pure xylazine: 15/15 positive at 2.5 µg/mL and above; 3/15 at 1 µg/mL (12 faint); 7/15 at 0.5 µg/mL (8 faint); 0/15 at 0.1 µg/mL. Cross-reactivity at 100 µg/mL: lidocaine only of 76 other compounds. Sisco et al. (2024b), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.

evidence.locator: Table 2, community-acquired drug residue rows and footnote c (p. 945); 3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples (p. 946)
evidence.extracted: Of 100 residue samples, 66 contained xylazine above the GC-MS/MS limit of detection. At or above 1 μg/ml: 37 of 38 positive, 1 negative (Sample 63, 2 μg/ml); below 1 μg/ml: 6 of 28 positive, 10 faint negative, 12 negative; not detected: 0 of 34 positive, 1 faint negative, 33 negative. Sensitivity 0.974, specificity 1.00 and accuracy 0.986, calculated only on samples above the cut-off or without xylazine. Editors' calculation on the study card: Wilson 95% CI 0.865–0.995 (sensitivity) and 0.898–1.000 (specificity); 43 of 66 xylazine-containing samples positive (0.65, 0.53–0.76).

evidence.locator: 3.2 Limit of detection, 1st paragraph; Table 2, pure xylazine rows and footnote a
evidence.extracted: Fifteen strips per concentration: all positive at 2.5 μg/ml and every higher level up to 5,000 μg/ml; at 1 μg/ml 3 positive and 12 faint negative; at 0.5 μg/ml 7 positive and 8 faint negative; at 0.1 μg/ml and in water all 15 negative. The authors put the approximate limit of detection at 2.5 μg/ml, slightly higher than the listed cut-off.

A panel of 77 compounds including xylazine, each at 100 μg/ml in water with two strips: only lidocaine gave a positive. Medetomidine, clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine (listed as α2-agonists in Table 1) did not react; the authors note that these would not be detected, potentially creating a false sense of safety, and that lidocaine may give false positives. Editors' count: 76 compounds other than xylazine.

evidence.locator: 2 Materials and methods, 2nd paragraph; 2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, 1st paragraph (p. 943); 3.5 Limitations (p. 946)
evidence.extracted: Residues were wiped with cotton swabs from used paraphernalia obtained in Maryland and Nevada as part of another project; strips were read and photographed in the laboratory; all strips came from a single production lot from a single maker; the authors note that people dissolve a few milligrams of actual powder, which may give higher concentrations and different cross-reactions than the residues studied.

evidence.locator: Results and Discussion › Limit of Detection, 2nd paragraph (AM p. 6); Cross-Reactivity, 2nd and 8th paragraphs (AM pp. 7–8); Table 1 footnote (AM p. 16); Table 2 (AM p. 17)
evidence.extracted: Xylazine strips with an antibody different from the earlier ones that cross-reacted with lidocaine: approximate limit of detection 1 µg/mL; no positive or faint result with any other compound in the 79-analyte panel, which included lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine and medetomidine; of 14 additional analytes, brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations.

evidence.extracted: After two weeks unopened at 55 °C, xylazine strips gave faint negatives at 1 μg/mL and needed 10 μg/mL to read positive consistently; all other strip types were still positive at their detection limits.

risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high for Sisco et al. (2024a) (study card): the headline accuracy leaves out the 28 samples with xylazine below the cut-off, 22 of which read negative or faint; how the residue samples were chosen and whether readers knew the GC-MS/MS results are not reported.

inconsistency.note: Both versions of the strip detected xylazine near 1 to 2.5 µg/mL; they differ on lidocaine, which the change of antibody explains.

indirectness.note: Residues swabbed from used equipment, one production lot, laboratory readers; the claim is about xylazine strips as people use them on powders or pills.

imprecision.note: 38 and 34 classified samples (intervals 86.5–99.5% and 89.8–100%); 15 strips per concentration for the limit; cross-reactivity rests on two strips per compound at one concentration, which is stated in the claim.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources; laboratory evaluations of test strips are not registered.

grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence on real residues against quantitative GC-MS/MS starts high; one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded. The two studies share their first author and laboratory and test different versions of the strip, so the status is replicated by the same team; the newer version rests only on an in-vitro study and alone would be capped at low.
